title: Small Bottle, Big Pipe: Quantifying and Addressing the Impact of Data Centers on Public Water Systems
novelty: Moves beyond annual water totals to peak withdrawals, treatment capacity and infrastructure costs.
usPolicyRelevance: Informs which peak-demand and capacity data utilities could request before approving connections and allocating costs.
limitation: Unreviewed scenarios depend on growth, cooling and capacity prices. Local analysis also needs drought supply and distribution constraints.
nextResearchQuestion: Do hourly meter records confirm modeled coincident peaks during heat waves?
plainLanguage: A small annual water share can still require very large pipes on the hottest days.
priorityReason: Adds a service-capacity perspective to this shortlist.

title: Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids
novelty: Extends average-grid accounting with hourly, network-constrained tests of emissions caused by changed electricity demand.
usPolicyRelevance: Informs research on additionality, siting, renewable procurement and verifiable demand-response incentives.
limitation: One modeled Western grid; simulated reductions are not measured field outcomes or long-term capacity effects.
nextResearchQuestion: Do results persist under observed dispatch, extreme weather and future generation investment?
plainLanguage: The model tests whether shifting computing changes power-plant operation enough to reduce electricity-related carbon emissions.
priorityReason: Makes emissions claims testable against changes in the electricity system.

title: Health-Informed Computing: Estimating and Addressing the Public Health Impact of Data Centers
studyType: Accepted manuscript · modeled health impacts · v4
novelty: Adds spatially distributed air-pollution health costs to assessments centered on electricity and carbon.
usPolicyRelevance: Supports testing health-impact reporting, pollution-aware computing and protections for affected counties beyond host communities.
limitation: CACM acceptance is reported on arXiv; final publication unverified. Modeled damages are not observed illness.
nextResearchQuestion: Can monitoring validate exposure changes when computing shifts across places and hours?
plainLanguage: Pollution from the power supply can affect people far from the data center.
priorityReason: Connects operational decisions to geographically unequal health burdens.

title: Environmental impact and net-zero pathways for sustainable artificial intelligence servers in the USA
novelty: Combines AI-server growth, grid evolution, cooling and location rather than extrapolating a single footprint intensity.
usPolicyRelevance: Frames comparisons of siting incentives, efficiency requirements and clean-electricity investment under uncertain growth.
limitation: Modeled rankings depend on grid forecasts and water accounting; technical potential does not establish community acceptance.
nextResearchQuestion: Which pathways remain preferable after adding transmission, permitting and distributional constraints?
plainLanguage: A more efficient server still needs a suitable location and cleaner electricity.
priorityReason: Links several policy levers within one explicitly conditional U.S. analysis.

title: The Unequal Burden of Environmental and Health Costs of Energy-Intensive Artificial Intelligence
novelty: Broadens operational footprint discussions to workers, mining, fabrication and waste-processing communities.
usPolicyRelevance: Offers a research agenda for life-cycle health assessments, surveillance, equitable siting and community participation.
limitation: Abstract-only appraisal; no new causal health study. October issue record was accessible by October 1.
nextResearchQuestion: Which exposures and benefits accumulate among the same vulnerable populations across the supply chain?
plainLanguage: People making and disposing of computing equipment also belong in the health discussion.
priorityReason: Prevents local policy research from overlooking upstream and downstream burdens.

title: The Cloud Next Door: Investigating the Environmental and Socioeconomic Strain of Datacenters on Local Communities
studyType: Published conference late-breaking work · exploratory primary study
novelty: Complements global resource totals with Northern Virginia community experience and decision-making power.
usPolicyRelevance: Motivates research on public participation, local infrastructure burdens and enforceable community-benefit commitments.
limitation: Preliminary mixed-methods case study; neither representative national opinion nor causal epidemiology.
nextResearchQuestion: Do communities with earlier participation secure different permit conditions and measurable exposure outcomes?
plainLanguage: A national electricity estimate does not explain what living beside a facility feels like.
priorityReason: Identifies questions that resource accounting alone cannot answer.

title: How sovereign control, decarbonization and energy costs shape public support for data centers
novelty: Tests combined ownership, climate and local-cost tradeoffs instead of treating support as a single attitude.
usPolicyRelevance: Provides a replicable experimental design for studying U.S. permitting preferences and proposed benefit arrangements.
limitation: German stated preferences cannot be transferred numerically to U.S. communities or actual permitting behavior.
nextResearchQuestion: How do U.S. preferences change when bill protections and independently verified water limits are specified?
plainLanguage: Residents weigh who operates a facility alongside its effects on bills and the environment.
priorityReason: Turns broad acceptance claims into testable policy-design questions.

title: Making AI Less 'Thirsty'
studyType: Published research article · modeled accounting examples
novelty: Extends carbon-focused model reporting to direct cooling water and electricity-related water across locations and times.
usPolicyRelevance: Helps design comparable workload disclosures and evaluate water-aware scheduling alongside carbon goals.
limitation: Examples use modeled intensities; there is no universal water-per-query value.
nextResearchQuestion: What reporting boundary and time resolution permit independent validation without exposing sensitive operations?
plainLanguage: Water used at a power plant matters too, and the same computing job can differ by location.
priorityReason: Connects familiar AI-use questions to defensible disclosure requirements.

title: The environmental footprint of data centers in the United States
studyType: Peer-reviewed primary study · spatial footprint model
novelty: Disaggregates aggregate resource accounting into facility and electricity-supply watersheds, revealing geographic tradeoffs.
usPolicyRelevance: Provides a baseline design for joint water-carbon siting research and cumulative watershed screening.
limitation: Uses 2018 inputs and annual-average power attribution; omits hardware manufacture and direct generator emissions.
nextResearchQuestion: How do updated facilities, hourly power flows and seasonal scarcity change siting conclusions?
plainLanguage: A facility can move part of its water burden to the places producing its electricity.
priorityReason: Establishes the spatial accounting needed to interpret newer studies.

title: Sources of data center energy estimates: A comprehensive review
novelty: Examines where estimates originate and whether their inputs can be checked, rather than producing another demand forecast.
usPolicyRelevance: Supports research on mandatory reporting fields, auditability and uncertainty requirements for utility planning.
limitation: Covers publications through 2021; identifies provenance problems without establishing which forecast is correct.
nextResearchQuestion: Which minimum disclosures most improve independent replication of facility and regional demand estimates?
plainLanguage: Several reports agreeing is less reassuring when they reuse the same hidden inputs.
priorityReason: Provides a quality-control foundation for evaluating newer policy evidence.
